subject: English
description: Mixed tense identification + correction; perfect, continuous, perfect-continuous

questions.stem: Identify correct tense usage: 'By the time you arrive, I ___ my work.'

options.option_text: Will finish (simple future)
Will have finished (future perfect)
Have finished (present perfect)
Am finishing (present continuous)

questions.explanation: FUTURE PERFECT (will have + V3) is used for an action that WILL BE COMPLETED before another future action / time. 'By the time' is a CLASSIC trigger phrase for future perfect — the work finishing comes BEFORE 'you arrive'. Structure: 'Subject + will have + past participle'. INSIGHT — there are 12 main tenses (3 times × 4 aspects: simple, continuous, perfect, perfect-continuous). Each has a unique TIME-MARKER: 'by the time / by 5 PM tomorrow' → future perfect; 'since/for + time' with 'have/has' → present perfect; 'while X was happening' → past continuous. Memorising trigger phrases is the fastest way to nail tense questions.
questions.subject: English

options.option_text: Worked (simple past) here also too
Has been working (present perfect continuous)
Was working (past continuous) here
Is working (present continuous) here

questions.explanation: Trigger phrase: 'SINCE 2010' = action started in past + still continues → PRESENT PERFECT or PRESENT PERFECT CONTINUOUS. PPC ('has/have been + V-ing') emphasises ONGOING duration — used here because work is continuous activity. Compare: 'I have lived here since 2010' (PP — focuses on completed state); 'I have been living here since 2010' (PPC — emphasises duration of activity). With ACTION verbs (work, study, run) + 'since/for' duration → PPC preferred. With STATIVE verbs (know, love, own, believe) → PP only ('I have known him since 2010'; never 'have been knowing'). INSIGHT — stative verbs don't take continuous tenses normally.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Identify error if any: 'I am knowing him for ten years.'

options.option_text: No error in the sentence here also
'Am knowing' is wrong; should be 'have known'
'For' should be replaced by 'since'
'Him' should be replaced by 'he' option

questions.explanation: ERROR: 'KNOW' is a STATIVE verb (mental state, not action) — does NOT take CONTINUOUS form. Correct: 'I HAVE KNOWN him for ten years' (Present Perfect). Other STATIVE verbs to remember: like, love, hate, believe, want, need, prefer, own, possess, belong, contain, consist, seem, appear (for senses), exist. Common Indian-English error: 'I am loving it' / 'I am understanding'. Standard English would say 'I love it' / 'I understand' (though 'I'm loving it' is now famous — McDonald's slogan, accepted in marketing). 'For 10 years' is fine here (duration). 'Since' would need a starting point ('since 2014'). Both OK in PP/PPC.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose: 'The patient ___ by the time the doctor arrived.'

options.option_text: Died (simple past)
Had died (past perfect)
Has died (present perfect)
Was dying (past continuous)

questions.explanation: PAST PERFECT ('had + V3') describes the EARLIER of two past events. Sequence: patient died (earlier) → doctor arrived (later). Use HAD DIED for the earlier event. STRUCTURE for sequencing past events: earlier event = past perfect; later event = simple past. INSIGHT — past perfect emphasises completion BEFORE another past moment. Same pattern: 'When I reached the station, the train had already left' (train leaving was earlier). Common ERRORS: students use simple past for both — but that loses the sequence info. PPC ('had been + V-ing') is the duration version: 'He had been waiting for an hour when she arrived'.
questions.subject: English

options.option_text: Is boiling (present continuous)
Boils (simple present, universal truth)
Has boiled (present perfect form)
Will boil (simple future tense)

questions.explanation: UNIVERSAL TRUTHS, scientific facts, habitual actions, general statements always use SIMPLE PRESENT — even though physically described action seems instantaneous or future. Other examples: 'The Sun rises in the east'; 'Honesty is the best policy'; 'Water freezes at 0°C'. INSIGHT — SIMPLE PRESENT covers: (1) universal truths (laws of nature); (2) habits ('I drink coffee daily'); (3) schedules ('the train leaves at 6 PM'); (4) commentary ('Tendulkar plays a perfect cover drive'); (5) headlines ('PM addresses Parliament'). NOT for actions in progress NOW (use present continuous). PYQ trap: confusing universal truth with continuous form.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose: 'When I was a child, I ___ to play cricket every evening.'

options.option_text: Use (simple present, wrong tense)
Used (past habit, 'used to')
Have used (present perfect form)
Was using (past continuous form)

questions.explanation: USED TO + base verb = PAST HABIT (something done regularly in past, not anymore). 'I used to play cricket' = I played cricket regularly back then. NEGATIVE: 'didn't use to' (no 'd' on use). NOT same as 'I am used to / get used to' (= 'accustomed to' + noun/gerund). 'I am used to spicy food' = accustomed; 'I used to eat spicy food' = past habit. WOULD also expresses past habits with action verbs only ('When I was 10, I would play cricket'). NOT WOULD with state verbs ('I would be tall' is wrong; use 'I used to be tall'). PYQ favourite distinction.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose: 'Look at those black clouds! It ___ rain soon.'

options.option_text: Will (simple future, prediction) here
Is going to (intentional/evidence-based future)
Rains (simple present tense) here option
Was raining (past continuous) here

questions.explanation: BE GOING TO + verb = future based on PRESENT EVIDENCE / intentions. 'Black clouds' = visible evidence → 'is going to rain'. WILL + verb = simple/spontaneous prediction or decision made at moment of speaking. Subtle but real distinction: 'I think it WILL rain' (just a guess); 'It is GOING TO rain' (clouds are evidence). Other future forms: PRESENT CONTINUOUS for plans ('I'm meeting her tomorrow'); SIMPLE PRESENT for schedules ('The train leaves at 6'); FUTURE PERFECT ('will have done') for completion before future point. INSIGHT — English future is rich: 5+ ways to express 'future', each subtly different. Choose by context.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: He said, 'I have finished my project.' Which of the following is the correctly reported version of this sentence?

options.option_text: He said that he has finished his project.
He said that he finished his project already.
He said that he had finished his project.
He said that he would finish his project soon.

questions.explanation: In reported speech, present perfect ('have finished') backshifts to past perfect ('had finished') when the reporting verb 'said' is past tense. Option A retains 'has finished', violating the backshift rule. Option D introduces 'would finish', wrongly implying the project may remain incomplete, which contradicts the original statement.

questions.stem: While the minister ___ his address, reporters quietly took notes in the gallery.

options.option_text: delivered, a simple past verb for a completed speech act
was delivering, a past continuous for an action in progress
had delivered, a past perfect for a prior completed action
delivers, a simple present tense used as historical present

questions.explanation: The conjunction 'while' signals that the minister's speech was an ongoing background action when reporters simultaneously took notes. Past continuous 'was delivering' correctly captures this in-progress quality. Option A ('delivered') treats both actions as equally completed, losing the continuity that 'while' requires and flattening the temporal overlap the sentence describes.

questions.stem: By the end of this month, Ramesh ___ in this hostel for exactly six continuous months.

options.option_text: will be staying, future continuous showing planned ongoing residence
will have stayed, future perfect focusing on completion not duration
would be staying, a conditional implying uncertainty about the stay
will have been staying, future perfect continuous for unbroken duration

questions.explanation: The phrase 'exactly six continuous months' stresses unbroken duration leading up to a specific future point, which is precisely what future perfect continuous expresses. Option B ('will have stayed') is a strong distractor — it is grammatically possible but highlights completion rather than the ongoing continuity that 'continuous months' demands. Option A ('will be staying') ignores the specified duration entirely.

questions.stem: She ___ the report before the manager called her in to present it to the board.

options.option_text: completed, treating both actions as simultaneous simple past events
had completed, showing the report was done before the manager's call
was completing, suggesting the task was still ongoing at call time
has completed, using present perfect for a recently finished task

questions.explanation: Completing the report happened earlier than the manager calling — the earlier of two past events takes past perfect. 'Had completed' establishes this sequence explicitly. Option A ('completed') is tempting since 'before' already signals order, but past perfect is the grammatically preferred and examiners' expected form. Option C wrongly implies the report was still unfinished when the call came.

questions.stem: If Reena ___ harder during her studies, she would be a senior IAS officer by now.

options.option_text: had worked, mixed conditional linking past effort to present outcome
worked, simple past used in a standard type-2 conditional clause
has worked, present perfect implying recent or current effort only
would have worked, incorrectly placing 'would' in the if-clause

questions.explanation: This is a mixed conditional: a past hypothetical condition (past perfect 'had worked' in the if-clause) paired with a present result ('would be… by now' — would + bare infinitive). Option B ('worked') fits a Type-2 conditional but only for a present/future hypothetical, not a past-to-present scenario. Option D is the classic Indian-exam error of placing 'would' inside the if-clause, which is always incorrect.

questions.stem: Identify the tense error in: 'The judge will deliver the verdict as soon as all evidence will be examined by both parties.'

options.option_text: 'will deliver' must be changed to 'delivers' as no future tense is allowed here
The sentence is correct; both uses of future tense are perfectly valid
'will be examined' should be 'is examined' — time clauses take simple present
'both parties' is redundant here and should be replaced with 'the parties'

questions.explanation: After time conjunctions (as soon as, when, before, after, until), future tense is never used — simple present replaces it. So 'will be examined' must become 'is examined'. The main clause 'will deliver' is perfectly correct; the restriction applies only to the subordinate time clause. Option A is a dangerous overgeneralisation: many candidates wrongly extend the rule to the main clause as well, making this a high-value discrimination point.

questions.stem: Which of the following sentences is FREE from any tense error or inconsistency?

options.option_text: She realized she forgot her keys only after the door shut behind her.
The letter which they have posted last Tuesday arrived at its destination.
He told his boss he will complete the task before the next meeting ends.
The project that we had been working on was finally completed last Friday.

questions.explanation: Option D is correct: 'had been working' (past perfect continuous) shows an action in progress before 'was completed' (simple past), with 'last Friday' anchoring both firmly in the past — a flawless tense sequence. Option A: 'forgot' must be 'had forgotten' since forgetting preceded 'realized'. Option B: 'have posted' (present perfect) directly clashes with 'last Tuesday' (specific past time marker — only simple past is used). Option C: after 'told' (past tense), backshift requires 'would complete', not 'will complete'.
